Newborn Care

Ibuprofen while breastfeeding: doses, precautions and pain relief

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Ibuprofen is often compatible with breastfeeding when an anti-inflammatory medicine is appropriate. Use the instructions for your own product and check your health history and the baby’s circumstances rather than avoiding all pain relief.

Pain relief and breastfeeding can often continue together

Ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicine, or NSAID, used for pain, inflammation and fever. It is commonly chosen during breastfeeding when this type of medicine is appropriate. Only a very small amount enters breast milk, and it does not usually build up in the baby during ordinary short-term use.

Compatibility with breastfeeding is only part of the decision. Your own medical history, the cause of the pain, other medicines and the baby’s health also matter. Guidance is most straightforward for a healthy baby born at term. Tell the pharmacist or prescriber if the baby was premature, is unwell or has a medical condition so they can assess the individual situation.

What the milk-transfer studies show

An often-cited 1984 study involved 12 patients taking 400 mg every six hours for pain after caesarean birth. The investigators estimated that less than 1 mg per day was excreted into milk under that study’s conditions. Early studies could not detect very low concentrations with their assays; later, more sensitive measurements confirmed that transfer is small rather than necessarily zero.

These findings support ibuprofen’s use during breastfeeding, but they are not a personal dosing schedule or proof that the maximum dose suits everyone. Comparing milk exposure with a fixed 50 mg infant dose is also misleading: a baby’s treatment dose depends on age, weight, formulation and clinical need. Keep research measurements separate from instructions for either patient.

How much to take: check the exact product

Use the lowest dose that works for the shortest necessary time, following your local label or prescription. As a UK example for common immediate-release adult tablets, NHS guidance allows 200 to 400 mg up to three times in 24 hours, leaving at least four hours between doses, with no more than 1,200 mg in 24 hours. This is not an instruction to take a dose every four hours throughout the day.

Other strengths, long-acting products and prescribed regimens may differ. Do not copy an old study’s six-hour schedule or increase a dose because milk transfer is low. Take tablets with water, ideally with or after food, and check how long self-treatment is allowed. If pain needs repeated treatment beyond the label’s limits, arrange a review. Seek prompt poison-service or medical advice if you take more than directed, even if you feel well.

You do not usually need to rearrange feeds

Medicines can pass from the bloodstream into milk, but the amount and timing differ between drugs. A claim about an ibuprofen blood-level peak one or two hours after a dose is not a reliable instruction for scheduling every breastfeed. With appropriate ordinary ibuprofen use, there is generally no need to wait a fixed interval before feeding.

You do not normally need to pump and discard milk, give formula or reserve previously expressed milk simply because you took ibuprofen. Feed the baby responsively. A premature or medically vulnerable baby, unusual dosing or several medicines together may need specialist advice, but a generic concern about any medicine in milk should not automatically interrupt breastfeeding.

Your health history and other medicines still matter

Check before taking ibuprofen if you have a current or previous stomach ulcer, gastrointestinal bleeding, kidney or significant heart disease, a bleeding disorder, or an allergy to aspirin or another NSAID. Asthma also matters, especially if aspirin or an anti-inflammatory has previously caused wheezing. Not everyone with asthma reacts, so a blanket claim that it always causes bronchospasm is inaccurate.

Tell the pharmacist about blood thinners, low-dose aspirin and all other medicines. Do not combine ibuprofen with another NSAID such as naproxen unless specifically instructed. Check cold-and-flu and combination pain products for duplicate ingredients. If you are pregnant or could be pregnant, say so: pregnancy precautions are different from breastfeeding advice, and breastfeeding compatibility does not make ibuprofen suitable throughout pregnancy.

Other pain medicines need their own assessment

Paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, is another commonly used pain-relief option during breastfeeding. A pharmacist can check which medicine best fits the symptoms and whether a combination is appropriate. Naproxen has a longer half-life and is generally limited to short-term use with infant monitoring when chosen; it is not simply interchangeable with ibuprofen for regular use.

Brand names alone are not enough because versions may contain different ingredients, including codeine or a decongestant. Herbal remedies and supplements also need checking. It is not necessary or helpful to avoid every medicine as an ideal: treating a parent’s health matters. Antidepressants, for example, are assessed individually, and some are compatible with breastfeeding. Do not stop prescribed mental-health treatment because of a blanket warning in an article.

Aspirin for pain and prescribed low-dose aspirin are different

Aspirin is not recommended as a routine painkiller during breastfeeding. A prescribed low-dose antiplatelet regimen for a specific medical reason is a different decision and can sometimes be used cautiously with monitoring. Do not start aspirin as an alternative to ibuprofen or stop a prescribed low-dose course without discussing the reason it was given.

Reye’s syndrome is a rare, serious illness associated with giving aspirin directly to children during viral illness. Whether negligible exposure through milk during low-dose maternal treatment could cause it is unknown; it should not be described as proven harm from every exposure. If the baby develops fever or a viral illness while you take prescribed aspirin, contact the responsible clinician promptly to review the medicine and feeding plan.

Avoid codeine and recognise serious infant symptoms

Codeine is not recommended during breastfeeding because conversion to morphine varies and the risks cannot be predicted reliably. A prescription does not automatically make it a suitable breastfeeding choice. If you have taken it accidentally, seek prompt advice about an alternative and any feeding or monitoring precautions needed for your situation.

A baby who is unusually difficult to wake, floppy, feeding poorly or breathing slowly needs immediate medical assessment, especially after possible opioid exposure. Call emergency services for breathing difficulty or marked unresponsiveness. Do not wait for the next routine appointment or assume that the baby is simply sleeping well.

The baby’s treatment is a separate decision

Ibuprofen reaching the baby through milk is not enough to treat the baby’s fever or pain. If the baby needs medicine, a clinician or pharmacist should check their age, weight, hydration and the product concentration. Do not give adult tablets or estimate a dose from the amount you take.

Maternal ibuprofen use does not usually require an automatic change to an otherwise appropriate infant prescription, but check both treatments with the baby’s care team. As a precaution, report persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, feeding changes or other worrying symptoms. Describe the timing and all medicines involved rather than deciding without assessment that breast milk is the cause.

Four everyday measures that may help a headache

Keep fluids and regular meals accessible. A drink and a simple snack near the feeding area may help when busy days lead to missed meals or thirst. Drink according to your needs; forcing extra water is not a guaranteed way to increase milk production.

Protect opportunities for rest. Another caregiver may be able to take over a settling period or household task so you can sleep. Rest should be practical support, not another demand that every parent must manage while the baby naps.

Gentle activity, such as a short walk, may support wellbeing when you feel ready and your recovery allows it. It is not a guaranteed cure for fatigue or a reason to exercise through pain. After a difficult birth or with ongoing symptoms, ask what level of activity is appropriate.

For muscle tension, try a comfortable feeding position and a wrapped cool pack on the neck if it helps. Keep ice off bare skin and stop if uncomfortable. Heat or cold may relieve some aches, but neither replaces assessment of a new, severe or persistent headache.

Treat the cause, not only the pain score

You do not have to endure untreated pain out of fear that all medicines harm a breastfed baby. At the same time, relief after a tablet does not prove that the cause is harmless. Arrange a review if headaches or other pain recur, need escalating doses or interfere with daily life.

After birth, seek urgent care for a severe or worsening headache, vision changes, chest pain, difficulty breathing, significant abdominal pain or fever of 38°C or higher. Mention that you recently gave birth. Vomiting blood, black tarry stools or a severe allergic reaction also needs urgent assessment. A safe pain plan includes knowing when self-care should give way to medical help.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Only very small amounts of ibuprofen enter milk; routine feed delays or milk disposal are generally unnecessary.

Breastfeeding compatibility does not override adult dosing limits or contraindications.

Codeine, aspirin for pain and prescribed low-dose aspirin need different advice.

How BeMama can help

Keep a list of active ingredients and doses, including combination products, so a pharmacist can check the whole pain-relief plan.

When to seek help

A baby who is floppy, hard to wake or breathing slowly needs emergency help. Severe postpartum headache, visual changes, chest pain or breathlessness also needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest appropriate time.
  • Read the exact product label, not only the brand.
  • A baby’s medicine dose is a separate decision.
  • Do not stop prescribed treatment without discussing it.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to stop breastfeeding after taking ibuprofen?

Usually not when taking an appropriate dose. Routine waiting, pumping and discarding milk or switching to formula is generally unnecessary.

Does the 400 mg every six hours study tell me my dose?

No. It was a research regimen, not a universal over-the-counter instruction. Follow your own label or prescription and individual medical advice.

Can I take a dose every four hours all day?

Not from the UK example in this article. The four-hour interval is a minimum gap, while the example also limits use to three doses and 1,200 mg in 24 hours. Your own product instructions govern.

Does having asthma always rule out ibuprofen?

No. Suitability depends on the history, particularly previous reactions to aspirin or NSAIDs. Check with a clinician or pharmacist before using it if unsure.

Can I combine ibuprofen and naproxen?

Do not combine two NSAIDs unless a clinician specifically directs it. Check other pain and cold products for duplicate ingredients too.

Can I use codeine if it was prescribed?

Codeine is not recommended during breastfeeding. Ask the prescriber for an appropriate alternative rather than assuming the prescription makes it suitable.

Should I stop prescribed low-dose aspirin?

Do not stop it on your own. Its purpose differs from aspirin for pain. Ask the responsible clinician to review the plan, particularly if the baby develops fever or viral symptoms.

Does my baby get a pain-relief dose through my milk?

No. Milk exposure is very small and does not treat the baby. Any infant medicine needs a separate age-, weight- and product-specific assessment.

Must I avoid antidepressants while breastfeeding?

No blanket rule applies. Some can be used; the particular medicine and circumstances need assessment. Do not abruptly stop prescribed mental-health treatment.

When is a postpartum headache more than a self-care problem?

A severe or worsening headache, particularly with visual changes or other concerning symptoms, needs urgent assessment. Tell the clinician that you recently gave birth.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
